passage: In the hospital billing office, Divyansh, the supervisor, watched the week unfold. Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday and stayed late on Thursday. Priya at the next desk printed the same three forms and spent long stretches at the tea counter. Nobody had complained. Divyansh noticed Anand's shoulders sagging and Priya's empty in-tray. He weighed it up: if he ignored it, Priya would keep coasting, and Anand would burn out. On Friday he asked Priya for a private word: "I want to understand your workload. Can we look at it together?" Then he took Anand aside and said, "I see how much you have done. Let me rebalance."

qa.q: How many claims did Anand reconcile by Wednesday?
qa.a: Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Divyansh worried about when weighing up what to do?
qa.a: Divyansh was concerned that ignoring the imbalance would reward coasting and burn out Anand; the worry was for fairness and for Anand's health.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do on Friday that a fair manager would do?
qa.a: Divyansh spoke privately with each person, asked Priya about the workload without accusing, and told Anand the effort was seen and would be rebalanced.

qa.q: What might Anand have felt when Divyansh said "I see how much you have done"?
qa.a: Anand probably felt relief and a little pride at being noticed after quietly carrying the load; sagging shoulders suggest that being unseen had been wearing.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and chooses a fair, private conversation over ignoring it.

passage: Dear Francis, I need an outside view. On my team of six, Rahul carries about half the work and Tessa produces about a fifth. I can see it every week in the tracker. Rahul never complains and Tessa always smiles in meetings. I have said nothing for two months, and last week Rahul stayed until nine and looked exhausted. I kept telling myself it would even out. It will not. Next week I will speak privately with each of them, first Tessa, to understand what is going on, then Rahul, to thank him and ask what he needs. Tell me if you think I am being unfair to either. — Zainab

qa.q: How long has Zainab said nothing about the uneven work?
qa.a: Zainab has said nothing for two months.

qa.q: What is Zainab feeling as writing that "it will not" even out?
qa.a: Zainab feels uneasy and a bit guilty for waiting so long, and resolved that ignoring the imbalance is not working.

qa.q: What plan does Zainab make about how to raise the issue?
qa.a: Zainab plans private conversations, first with Tessa to understand what is going on, then with Rahul to thank him and ask what he needs.

qa.q: What might Rahul be feeling after staying until nine while never complaining?
qa.a: Rahul probably feels exhausted and perhaps unnoticed, and may also worry that complaining would look bad; the tiredness shows in staying late.

grounding: A manager sees one person doing heavy lifting and another barely contributing, and plans a fair, private conversation.
